abstract.t: This document describes an API to query a network regarding its Energy Traffic Ratio for a given path.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: Energy management is becoming one of the major societal goals for the next decade, and networks are one of the major consumers of energy nowadays. Energy management of network services is thus one of the forefronts of innovation and action from network service stakeholders, involving manufacturers, operators and customers. In this line, there is a shared goal of achieving better energy awareness.

As with any other network metric, the energy traffic ratio could be collected from the underlying network infrastructure. However, there is not a common or single definition of energy metrics towards network consumers so that can be uniformly reported, particularly in heterogeneous network scenarios. This document introduces an API to query networks about Energy Traffic Ratio.

section.title: Terminology and Requirements Notation
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.title: Path Energy Traffic Ratio API (PETRA)
section.t: This documents describes an API to query a network about the Energy Traffic Ratio for a given path. It takes as input the source and destination of a path along with the traffic throughput between and returns energy information related to the traffic on the path. This is energy computed by the infrastructure that is dynamically part of the traffic path. The API is agnostic to the actual hops and underlaying infrastructure that enables a path, which might change transparently to the API. This document only describes the API, the computation of the energy information to return is out of the scope of this document. In the current version of this document, source and destination endpoints can be IP addresses, IP prefixes, or MAC addresses.

section.title: Energy Information
section.t: This API allows to return a number of energy attributes associated with the path and the traffic. Currently the parameters that could be returned as energy information as part of the query are:

ul.li: Watts per Gigabit: How many Watts are consumed per Gigabit of traffic traversing the path.

section.title: Recursive Usage
section.t: The API is envisioned in such a way that could be used recursively. That means, subpaths could report their energy consumption using PETRA and such energy consumption could be aggregated and reported for the overall path also using PETRA.

Similarly, this API could be (recursively) used to provide energy information according to the definition of Service Models in an SDN context as described in . In that case, using Figure 3 in as reference (below), PETRA could be used between the Controller(s) and the Network Orchestrator(s), between the Network Orchestrator(s) and the Service Orchestrator, and between the Service Orchestrator and the Customer(s).

section.t: While considering recursive usage, the aspect of double-counting shall also be taken into consideration. Double counting refers to the fact of counting more than once the same energy consumed. Organizations using PETRA in a recursive manner need to take appropriate measures to ensure no double-counting occurs across recursive calls to the API.

section.t: This is a posible definition of PETRA as a module following the YANG specification . The module uses the common YANG data types defined in , and imports the network slice model from and the power and energy model from .

section.title: Module Definition
section.t: Validation of this module depends on the exact revision set of imported modules and transitive dependencies in the validation environment. In particular, errors about missing TE packet-type groupings (for example, one-way-performance-metrics-gauge-packet and two-way-performance-metrics-gauge-packet) originate in external module dependencies and need to be addressed by aligning dependency revisions in the toolchain.

module ietf-petra {
  yang-version 1.1;
  namespace "urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-petra";
  prefix ietf-petra;

    prefix ietf-inet-types;
    reference "RFC 9911: Common YANG Data Types";
  }

  import ietf-yang-types {
    prefix ietf-yang-types;
    reference "RFC 9911: Common YANG Data Types";
  }

  import ietf-network-slice-service {
    prefix ietf-nss;

      "draft-ietf-teas-ietf-network-slice-nbi-yang-26:

/*
    If you have an implementation of this YANG module, you could
    access it like something this over RESTCONF:

    $ curl --location --request POST \
      'https://localhost:8008/restconf/operations/ietf-petra:energy/query' \
      --header 'Content-Type: application/yang-data+json' \
      --user 'admin:admin' \
      --data-raw '{
          'input' : {
              'source': {
                  'ip-prefix': '10.10.10.0/24'
              },
              'destination': {
                  'ip-prefix': '10.20.20.0/24'
              },
              'throughput': '40'
          }
        }'

    And if all goes well, you might receive (besides all the
    HTTP headers) a reply body with something like this:

    {
      'output': {
        'success': {
          'watts-per-gigabit': '191.855'
        }
      }
    }

    description
      "Initial YANG rendition of the PETRA Energy API, v1.0.1";
    reference
      "RFC XXXX: ...";
  }

  grouping endpoint {
    description
      "Identifies one endpoint of an energy-measurement path.";
    choice identifier {
      mandatory true;
      description
        "Endpoint represented as an IP address, IP prefix, MAC address,
        or Service Demarcation Point (SDP) identifier.";
      case ip-address {
        leaf ip-address {
          type ietf-inet-types:ip-address;
          mandatory true;
          description
            "IPv4 or IPv6 address.";
        }
      }
      case ip-prefix {
        leaf ip-prefix {
          type ietf-inet-types:ip-prefix;
          mandatory true;
          description
            "IPv4 or IPv6 network prefix.";
        }
      }
      case mac-address {
        leaf mac-address {
          type ietf-yang-types:mac-address;
          mandatory true;
          description
            "IEEE 802 MAC address.";
        }
      }
      case sdp-id {
        leaf sdp-id {
          type leafref {
            path "/ietf-nss:network-slice-services"
               + "/ietf-nss:slice-service"
               + "/ietf-nss:sdps"
               + "/ietf-nss:sdp"
               + "/ietf-nss:id";
            require-instance true;
          }
          mandatory true;
          description
            "Reference to a Service Demarcation Point (SDP) within the
            scope of a Network Slice Controller (NSC).";
        }
      }
    }
  }

  grouping energy-metrics {
    description
      "Grouping for query result metrics.";
    leaf watts-per-gigabit {
      type decimal64 {
        fraction-digits 3;
      }
      units W/Gb;
      description
        "Watts consumed per Gigabit transmitted";
    }
    leaf data-source-accuracy {
      type identityref { base eo:data-source-accuracy; }
      description
        "Accuracy classification of the watts-per-gigabit value,
        using the GREEN data-source-accuracy hierarchy.
        Implementations SHOULD populate this leaf to enable
        consumers to assess reliability. For path-aggregated
        values derived from multiple components, the RECOMMENDED
        value is the LEAST accurate accuracy class among all
        contributing energy objects.";
    }
  }

  container energy {
    description
      "PETRA API top level container.";
    action query {
      description
        "Query the network for energy consumption";
      input {
        must "throughput or (time-window/start-time and
              time-window/end-time and data-transmitted)" {
          error-message
            "Provide either throughput or a time window with start
            and end times together with data-transmitted.";
        }
        container source {
          description
            "Source endpoint.";
          uses endpoint;
        }
        container destination {
          description
            "Destination endpoint.";
          uses endpoint;
        }
        choice traffic-characterization {
          default throughput;
          description
            "Characterizes the traffic either by its throughput or by
            the amount of data transmitted during a time window.";
          case throughput {
            leaf throughput {
              type decimal64 {
                fraction-digits 3;
              }
              units Gb/s;
              description
                "Throughput between source and destination
                (in gigabits per second).";
            }
          }
          case time-window-and-data-transmitted {
            container time-window {
              description
                "Interval during which the data was transmitted.";
              leaf start-time {
                type ietf-yang-types:date-and-time;
                mandatory true;
                description
                  "Start date and time of the interval.";
              }
              leaf end-time {
                type ietf-yang-types:date-and-time;
                mandatory true;
                description
                  "End date and time of the interval.";
              }
            }
            leaf data-transmitted {
              type decimal64 {
                fraction-digits 3;
              }
              units Gb;
              mandatory true;
              description
                "Amount of data transmitted between source and
                destination during the time window (in gigabits).";
            }
          }
        }
      }
      output {
        choice result {
          description
            "Choice of which kind of result the query gave.";
          container success {
            description
              "Successful operation";
            uses energy-metrics;
          }
          container invalid-endpoint {
            presence
              "Indicates that an invalid endpoint was supplied.";
            description
              "Invalid source or destination endpoint supplied.";
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

section.title: Operational Considerations
section.t: This section highlights deployment and operations considerations for PETRA, following the guidance in .

ul.li: Measurement method impact: PETRA results can differ depending on whether values are directly measured, estimated, or model-derived. Operators SHOULD document the methodology used for each exposed metric.

Consumer intent differences: customer-facing use cases (for example, SD-WAN visibility and SLA reporting) prioritize repeatability and explainability, while operator optimization use cases may prioritize freshness and control-loop responsiveness.

Recursive aggregation and double counting: recursive or multi-domain use of PETRA can count the same contribution more than once. Implementations SHOULD define aggregation boundaries and controls that avoid double counting across segments and administrative domains.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: The YANG module defined in this document is specified and reviewed following the guidance in . PETRA query exchanges can reveal operationally sensitive information related to endpoints, traffic, and energy behavior, and therefore require careful deployment controls.
When this API is exposed over NETCONF or RESTCONF , implementations inherit those protocols' security properties and deployment requirements.
Implementations and deployments SHOULD consider at least the following:

ul.li: Secure transport: confidentiality and integrity protection for PETRA exchanges MUST be provided by the underlying management protocol and transport.
Authentication and authorization: servers MUST authenticate clients and MUST enforce authorization before processing requests.
Input validation: implementations SHOULD validate endpoint identifiers and traffic characterization values to prevent invalid requests and abusive workloads.
Information disclosure control: returned energy metrics can expose sensitive operational behavior and SHOULD be filtered according to policy and client privileges.
Denial-of-service resilience: implementations SHOULD apply protections such as rate-limiting, quotas, and bounded processing to protect control-plane resources.
Privacy: where measurements can be correlated to customer behavior, operators SHOULD minimize retention and protect logs and telemetry generated by queries.

section.title: Use Cases
section.t: This section describes some use-cases where this specification might be useful.

section.title: SD-WAN
section.t: Software-Defined Wide-Area Networks (SD-WAN) have become a common way for enterprises to provide cost-effective connectivity across their different geographically distributed sites. Typically, SD-WAN deployments operate as an overlay network that is established on top of an existing underlay connectivity network. One aspect to consider is that in many SD-WAN production deployments the operator of the overlay network and the operator of the underlay network are different organizations.

This poses an additional challenge when trying to derive energy metrics. Even if the underlay network is instrumented to collect energy data, this data is opaque to the operator of the overlay network which has no access to underlay information. While operators of underlay networks offer certain general network metrics to overlay operators, no interface has been defined to allow the overlay operator to query the underlay network for energy information.

In this context, the PETRA specification presented in this document enables the operator of the SD-WAN network to coordinate with the underlay operator to capture energy data. This in turns opens further use-cases, from observability and reporting to potentially overlay policies based on underlay energy data, further enabling an overall more energy-efficient operation of the network.

In addition to energy considerations in SD-WAN deployments, PETRA can also be leveraged for broader energy-aware service routing. In this context, network controllers and service orchestrators, such as SD-WAN controllers, transport SDN controllers, 5G slice orchestrators, or multi-domain service orchestrators, can use PETRA metrics not only to balance latency, throughput, or load, but also to optimize path selection according to energy-efficiency objectives. For example, paths with the lowest energy-consumption could be preferred, enabling service differentiation where energy-efficient paths are explicitly prioritized. This extends the SD-WAN use case into a more general paradigm where routing decisions are jointly driven by network performance and energy impact.

section.title: Multilayer Energy Management
section.t: The concept of multilayer L3-L1 collection involves integrating data from different network layers to provide a comprehensive view of network operations. The use case of multilayer involves collecting and correlating data from Layer 3 (network layer) down to Layer 1 (physical layer). This multilayer approach allows for better network performance, optimization, and troubleshooting by providing end-to-end visibility.

Leveraging PETRA API for multilayer L3-L1 collection use case enhances energy management by providing comprehensive visibility, enabling optimization, and supporting proactive management. This makes PETRA a useful tool for more accurate, efficient and effective energy management in modern networks.

section.title: SLA Negotiation for Energy-Efficient Services
section.t: Another use case for PETRA could the negotiation of Service Level Agreements (SLAs) between operators and enterprise customers. By exposing PETRA-derived metrics such as energy consumption, renewable energy percentage, providers can offer differentiated SLAs that explicitly include environmental targets. This enables customers to select network services not only based on performance guarantees (e.g. latency), but also on their environmental footprint (or a combination of both). For example requesting that at least 60% of traffic be carried over renewable-powered infrastructure. Such SLAs empower customers to align their digital services with corporate energy-efficient and sustainability goals and reporting requirements, while operators can use PETRA as the trusted source of verifiable energy data.

section.title: Requirements for Energy Efficiency Management
section.t: The document Framework for Energy Efficiency Management describes a reference model for energy management. The model includes an 'API Service Interface', labeled as interface (g) in the document, which "enables access for service consumption, enabling data retrieval, control, and integration through API".

In that context, PETRA is one example of such 'API Service Interface'. In the particular case of PETRA, the API might be used to consume from the Network controller, the Domain controller, or both. describes a few use-cases that could make use of PETRA as an 'API Service Interface' within the Framework for Energy Efficiency Management .
